title: I made a browser 4X game with Claude Opus 5.5, plus the editor I built to make it
author: Pristine_Good7326
selftext:
I used Claude Opus 5.5 for almost all of this, so I'll start there.   
  
The game is called NETA-S, a turn-based Civ-style 4X game that runs in the browser.  
  
You can try it here: nothing is required: [https://neta.art/w/kingdomrushdev/neta-s-release/neta-s](https://neta.art/w/kingdomrushdev/neta-s-release/neta-s)

It didn't start as a game. I first built a small editor called Cividot because I was tired of hand-editing rule data every time I changed something.   
  
It's on GitHub if you want to look at it: [https://github.com/tbj114/cividot](https://github.com/tbj114/cividot)

Cividot is a bit like RPG Maker, but for 4X. You edit techs and units, paint the map, write events, hit test play, and export a standalone build without touching engine code. The rules live in a C++17 engine I called Forge4X. The Godot 4.7.2 client only draws state and sends input back. I split it that way on purpose so the map view and the rules can't drift apart.

NETA-S is the first real game I made with it. There are three ages (Antiquity, Exploration, Modern). Your leader stays with you the whole run, and your civ changes each age. At 60 percent of an age a crisis hits, Builders are gone, and new settlements start as towns that make gold. Those were my attempts to fix the usual late-game snowball.

My favorite part is the **Leader Forge** on the title screen. You type a plain-English description of a leader you want to play, and a "Court Scribe" LLM turns it into an actual playable leader with a painted portrait (`gpt-image-2.5`).

The catch is that the LLM isn't allowed to make up fake mechanics. Every ability gets mapped to the 25 real effect types inside Forge4X, clamped to a max power budget of 2.5 across at most 3 effects, and validated by the engine's `check_rules` check. Ask for "flying ships" and the engine gives you faster naval units, plus a note from the scribe explaining why.

All the 3D art is CC0 packs (Kenney, Quaternius) re-graded with a Python script to match a slate, brass, and parchment UI. I also spent the last update obsessing over map feel: cursor-locked ground dragging, 80ms release inertia, and right-click multi-turn marching.

Since our whole build pipeline runs in a Linux sandbox on software rendering (`llvmpipe` and headless Chrome + SwiftShader), we tested it with automated click-through runs (`--ages-autotest`) and full AI-vs-AI games, but I'm curious how the web build runs on different real GPUs.
